title: Sikhs of Assam
hookLine: a community in Assam traces itself to soldiers who stayed long ago

lines: RICE FIELDS AND A NISHAN SAHIB.
cards: Rice fields in the Brahmaputra valley, green to the edge of the sky. A village gurdwara with a small Nishan Sahib above the trees.
Inside, the Ardas is said in Punjabi, but outside, the children run home calling to each other in Assamese. Their grandmothers wear the mekhela, the Assamese wrap. Their fathers tie turbans.
Ask the elders where the family came from, and the answer reaches back a long way, to men who marched east from Punjab and never marched home. These are the Sikhs of Assam.

teach.b: Start with the community's own memory. Tradition says soldiers from Punjab were sent east to help a king of Assam in a time of war. When the fighting was done, some of them didn't go back.
They stayed, married into Assamese families, farmed the land, and built gurdwaras in their villages.

teach.h: ASSAMESE IN LANGUAGE, SIKH IN FAITH.
teach.b: Their descendants are Assamese by language, food and dress, and Sikh by faith. There's an older thread too.

Sikh tradition remembers Guru Tegh Bahadur traveling to Assam, and a gurdwara on the Brahmaputra keeps that memory. So in the panth's telling, the Guru's footsteps reached the valley before the soldiers did.

teach.h: KEEPING THE FAITH FAR FROM PUNJAB.
teach.b: Being a Sikh far from Punjab has its own weight.

A community like this has to keep Gurmukhi alive among children who think in another language, keep the rehat where few neighbors know what a kara or a turban means, and stay connected to a panth whose center is a long journey away.
And yet this is also an old Sikh story. The Gurus traveled, and sangats grew in places where they stopped.

teach.h: ANG 450: WHERE THE GURU SITS IS BEAUTIFUL.
teach.b: Guru Ram Das sings, in a hymn on Ang 450, in paraphrase: wherever my true Guru goes and sits, that place becomes beautiful. A rice village in Assam is far from Amritsar.
In the logic of that line, it's not far from the Guru. The Granth sits there, the Ardas is said there, and the place is made beautiful by it.
Those who stayed far away didn't leave the Guru behind; they carried the Guru with them, and set the Granth down in new ground.

how: Sikhs of Assam keep village gurdwaras in the Brahmaputra valley, say the Ardas and read the Guru Granth Sahib, and live their daily lives in Assamese language, food and dress.

games.q: you're a soldier from Punjab, far east in Assam. the fighting is over. what does the community's tradition say some soldiers did?
o: stayed, married into Assamese families, and built gurdwaras.
games.why: they stayed, farmed the land, and set the Granth down in new ground. their descendants are Assamese and Sikh.

practice: Let a face come to mind: someone who made a home far from where their family began, a grandparent who crossed an ocean, a friend who moved for work.
Breathe in and see them there with what they carried, a recipe, a language, a prayer, and breathe out a little warmth across the distance.

wordCard.voice: Sikhs of Assam. A community in the Brahmaputra valley that traces itself, by tradition, to soldiers from Punjab who stayed. Assamese in language and dress, Sikh in faith. Today's word.
